query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding trace levels of Hf to a eutectic high‐entropy alloy promotes the formation of finely dispersed Hf-rich precipitates along the lamellar colony boundaries that pin dislocations and inhibit microcrack nucleation, thereby simultaneously enhancing room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) as conventionally cast and processed, exhibiting numerous internal boundaries prone to microcracking under room-temperature tension.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small, trace addition (approximately 0.5 atomic percent) of Hf into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation using identical processing routes as the baseline alloy (e.g., casting and standard thermo-mechanical treatments) to isolate the effect of Hf addition.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of Hf-rich intermetallic precipitates localized at or near the phase boundaries within the lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The Hf-rich precipitates act as strong pinning sites that restrict dislocation motion and impede the initiation and propagation of microcracks along the internal boundaries. This dual role of precipitation strengthening and boundary stabilization improves both the yield strength and the tensile ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Hf-modified alloy is expected to exhibit an increased tensile yield and ultimate strength along with enhanced plastic strain before failure at room temperature.
generation.baseline: The conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy without Hf addition, which typically shows a tradeoff between strength and ductility due to microcrack formation at the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.boundary: The expected benefits are associated with eutectic high-entropy alloys having lamellar dual-phase microstructures processed under conditions that permit the formation of fine precipitates. The effect may vary if the concentration of Hf is significantly different or if alternate processing routes alter precipitate morphology.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Hf concentration for achieving the best balance of strength and ductility is not firmly established, and there is uncertainty regarding the reproducibility of precipitate size/distribution, which might affect the mechanical outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy using identical casting and thermo-mechanical processing: one with a trace addition (~0.5 at.%) of Hf and one without. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and detailed microstructural characterizations (e.g., SEM/TEM) to assess precipitate distribution and microcrack formation.
measurements: Precipitate morphology and distribution at internal boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-doped samples do not show a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the expected fine Hf-rich precipitates at the lamellar interfaces correlating with reduced microcrack density, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

The strengthening effect of Hf on the alloy could be maintained at 600 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C.At different high temperatures, the Hf0.5 alloy exhibited a higher strength and ductility than the Hf0 alloys. The outstanding high-temperature strength of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the precipitation strengthening of the Hf-rich phase precipitated in the inner of the B2 phase. The excellent high-temperature ductility of the Hf0.5 alloy was attributed to the pinning effect of the Hf-rich phase that existed at grain and phase boundaries to boundary sliding during the high-temperature deformation.
